paragraphs.heading: Scattered background light
paragraphs.text: The Sunyaev–Zeldovich effect, or SZ effect, is named after Rashid Sunyaev and Yakov Zeldovich, who predicted it. It is a distortion in the spectrum of the cosmic microwave background (CMB), caused by high-energy electrons in galaxy clusters. When a low-energy CMB photon collides with one of these electrons, the photon gains energy on average. This kind of scattering is called inverse Compton scattering.

paragraphs.heading: Why astronomers care
paragraphs.text: The effect matters a great deal to both astrophysics and cosmology. It helps find new galaxy clusters, study their structure and mass, and pin down the Hubble constant. Since it is a scattering effect, its size does not depend on redshift. That means a cluster at high redshift can be found as easily as one at low redshift.

paragraphs.heading: The thermal effect
paragraphs.text: The thermal SZ effect is the distortion made by a large number of high-energy electrons, and it is mostly studied in galaxy clusters. Comparing it with X-ray emission from a cluster shows the cluster's thermal structure. If the temperature profile is known, SZ data can also give the cluster's baryonic mass along the line of sight. The same comparison, through the cluster's angular diameter distance, can yield the Hubble constant. In superclusters the signal is weak, under 8 μK, yet precise measurements can hint at how large-scale structure formed.

paragraphs.heading: The kinematic effect
paragraphs.text: The kinematic SZ effect appears when a galaxy cluster moves relative to the Hubble flow. It offers a way to work out the cluster's peculiar velocity. Written as Δ Tₖᵢₙ = −T_CMB Vₚ/c τ, it uses Vₚ for the peculiar velocity and τ for the optical depth. To use this, the thermal and kinematic effects first have to be pulled apart. For most galaxy clusters, the kinematic signal is fairly weak.

paragraphs.heading: Hard to see
paragraphs.text: Observing the effect is difficult, because its amplitude is small and it is easily confused with experimental error and other CMB temperature fluctuations. To tell a cluster's SZ effect apart from ordinary density perturbations, astronomers use both how the fluctuations depend on frequency and how they are laid out across the sky. Any analysis of CMB data at high angular resolution also has to allow for the effect.

paragraphs.heading: From first hint to hundreds of clusters
paragraphs.text: In 1984, teams from the Cambridge Radio Astronomy Group and Owens Valley Radio Observatory were the first to detect the effect in galaxy clusters. Ten years later, the Ryle Telescope made the first image of a cluster in the SZ effect. Two instruments were built just for it, and both saw first light in 2005: the Sunyaev–Zeldovich Array, and an SZ camera on the Atacama Pathfinder Experiment. In 2012 the Atacama Cosmology Telescope made the first statistical detection of the kinematic effect, and that year it was also seen for the first time in a single object, MACS J0717.5+3745. By 2015 the South Pole Telescope had used the effect to discover 415 galaxy clusters.
